unit.title: Perform manual metal arc welding process to AWS specification (Alloy steel pipe)

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A pipe job is to be welded "to AWS specification". What does this mean for the welding team?
options: Any method may be used as long as the welds look neat
The work must meet that AWS standard's rules
The pipe must be bought from an American supplier
Only welders trained in America may weld the pipe

questions.stem: In the electrode classification E8018-B2, what do the digits "80" tell you?
options: Use about 80 A on a 3.2 mm electrode
The coating is 80% iron powder by weight
Bake the electrodes at 80 °C before use
Minimum tensile strength about 80 000 psi

questions.stem: In the classification E8018-B2, what does the suffix "B2" tell you?
options: The weld metal is a chromium-molybdenum alloy
It is the second batch made that year
It may only be used in the flat position
It must be used on DC electrode negative

It can stay out of the oven for 18 hours
All positions; low-hydrogen iron powder coat

questions.stem: Why must low-hydrogen electrodes be used on chromium-molybdenum (Cr-Mo) alloy steel pipe?

They are cheaper than the cellulosic electrodes

questions.stem: A welder suggests an E6010 cellulosic root on Cr-Mo pipe, as used on carbon steel line pipe. Why is that a poor choice?

In a bucket of water to keep them cool

questions.stem: Low-hydrogen electrodes were left out in damp air overnight. What should be done with them?
options: Use them, because the flux dries out in the arc
Re-dry them as the maker says, or scrap them
Dip them in water so that the flux sets hard

questions.stem: Why is preheat applied before welding Cr-Mo pipe?

To burn the paint off the outside of the pipe

To slow cooling and let hydrogen escape

questions.stem: Where should the preheat temperature be checked?

On the parent metal by the joint, as the WPS says

On the welding bench next to the pipe

questions.stem: A temperature-indicating crayon marked 150 °C is rubbed on the pipe and melts. What does this tell you?

The pipe is at exactly 100 °C

options: Keep the joint within that range

Heat the pipe as hot as the torch allows

questions.stem: Why is heat treatment after welding often required on Cr-Mo pipe welds?

questions.stem: If heat treatment cannot start straight after welding, what does a WPS often say to do with the joint?

Leave it in the open breeze to cool quickly
Wrap it in insulation so that it cools slowly
Cover it in oil to stop rust from forming

questions.stem: A common pipe bevel is 37.5° on each pipe end. What is the included angle of the groove?
Why is a root face (land) ground on the bevelled pipe end?
options: To make the bevel angle bigger
To remove the need for a root gap
To help the pipe slide into the clamp
To control burn-through in the root

questions.stem: What is "hi-lo" on a pipe fit-up?

questions.stem: Before cutting pipe for a Cr-Mo job, how do you make sure it is the right material?

Look at the colour of the rust on the outside of the pipe
Tap it with a hammer and listen to the sound it makes
Check that the size matches the size on the drawing

1 hour 12 minutes

questions.stem: In the 5G position with low-hydrogen electrodes, which way is the pipe welded?

Round the pipe in one clockwise run

Give the weld a colour for the inspector
Cool the root quickly so that it hardens
Measure the root gap for the weld record

questions.stem: Which arc length is correct with low-hydrogen electrodes?
options: A long arc, to keep the electrode cool
A short arc, to keep shielding good
A very long arc with a whipping motion

questions.stem: Low-hydrogen welds show porosity at the start of each run. Which technique helps?
options: Strike on the finished weld and drag away fast
Hold a long arc for a few seconds after striking
Strike on the pipe surface outside, then move in

options: They use up electrodes and slow the job
They leave marks the paint will not cover

questions.stem: Why does the WPS limit the weave width of low-hydrogen fill and cap passes?

questions.stem: A welder passes a 6G pipe test. Generally, which positions does this qualify them for?
options: All positions, within the test's other limits
Only the 6G position on the same pipe size

Only vertical-up welding on plate

questions.stem: Which document shows that a welding procedure has been tested and passed?

questions.stem: During visual inspection, which cap condition would normally be rejected?

questions.stem: Which non-destructive test is most used to find buried slag and lack of fusion in pipe butt welds?

questions.stem: After heat treatment, why might the weld and the area next to it be hardness tested?
options: To find the colour grade of the weld
To check the height of the weld cap

To confirm the heat treatment worked

questions.stem: From a 6G pipe test coupon, why are bend test strips cut from set places around the pipe?
options: So that the cut pieces fit the bending machine

To cut down the number of tests that are needed

questions.stem: Radiography shows a slag inclusion in a Cr-Mo pipe weld. What is the correct way to repair it?
options: Repair to an approved procedure and re-test
Weld another cap over the top to bury the slag
Heat the area and hammer it to close the flaw
Grind the cap flush so that the X-ray cannot see it

questions.stem: Which polarity is normally used for E8018-B2 on a DC welding set?
options: DCEN (electrode negative)
DCEP (electrode positive)

questions.stem: Why should the electrode holding oven be checked at the start of each shift?
options: To count the electrodes for the cost report
To check that it is clean enough to look at
To dry the welders' gloves before work starts
To confirm it is on and at the right temperature

questions.stem: Welding Cr-Mo pipe gives off fume containing chromium and manganese. Which control is best in the Centre's booth?
options: A fan blowing hard across the arc

questions.stem: Pipe is being preheated with an oxy-fuel heating torch. Which precaution matters most?
options: Heat one spot until it glows red, to save time
Lay the gas cylinders flat on the floor while heating

questions.stem: Electric resistance heating pads are used for preheat and heat treatment. Who should set up and run them?
options: Any trainee who has watched it done once
The client's driver when he is on site
A trained, authorised heat-treatment operator

questions.stem: Why use a line-up (pipe) clamp when fitting pipe for welding?
options: To hold the ends in line with an even gap
To heat the pipe ends evenly before welding
To earth the pipe to the welding machine
To bevel the pipe ends at the right angle

questions.stem: A team member skips the preheat because "the weather is hot". As team leader, what should you do?
options: Stop the work, preheat to the WPS and check what was welded
Accept it, because the air in Jamaica is warm enough
Let them carry on, but tell them to weld more slowly

questions.stem: Which record shows the preheat and interpass temperatures actually used on each joint?
options: The material order form
The tool store sign-out sheet
The weld and heat log for the joint

questions.stem: Why is each pipe weld given its own number and marked on the drawing?
options: So that the welder can be paid by the joint
So that the client can pick a favourite weld
So that the pipe does not need a heat number

questions.stem: A pipe joint needs about 1.2 kg of deposited weld metal. If about 60% of the electrode weight ends up as weld metal, about how many kg of electrodes are needed?
options: 2.0 kg
1.8 kg

questions.stem: Pipe welding is being done outside and it starts to rain. What should happen?
options: Carry on, because the preheat will dry the pipe

essays.stem: Explain why chromium-molybdenum (Cr-Mo) alloy steel pipe is harder to weld than carbon steel pipe, and how the welding procedure deals with each problem.
essays.modelAnswer: Cr-Mo steel hardens easily. When the weld cools quickly, the heat-affected zone next to it can become hard and brittle. If hydrogen gets into the weld, it can cause cracks in that hard zone, often hours after welding (hydrogen or cold cracking). The procedure deals with this in several ways. It calls for low-hydrogen electrodes of a matching alloy, such as E8018-B2, kept dry in an oven, and never cellulosic electrodes. It sets a minimum preheat, which slows cooling and helps hydrogen escape. It sets a maximum interpass temperature, so the joint does not overheat. It may say to keep the heat on or cool slowly under insulation after welding. It usually calls for heat treatment after welding, to temper the hard zone and relieve stresses. The joint must also be clean and dry, because rust, oil, paint and moisture all bring hydrogen. Material identification is important, because the wrong filler on the wrong pipe can fail in service.
markingPoints: Hardens easily: hard, brittle HAZ on fast cooling
Hydrogen cracking risk in the hard zone
Low-hydrogen matching electrodes kept dry; no cellulosic
Preheat, interpass limit and slow cooling
Heat treatment after welding; clean dry joint; correct material identification

essays.stem: Describe how low-hydrogen alloy electrodes should be stored, handled and used on a pipe job, and explain why.
essays.modelAnswer: Low-hydrogen electrodes pick up moisture from the air, and moisture brings hydrogen into the weld, which can cause cracking in alloy steel. Sealed tins are kept in a dry store until needed. Once opened, the electrodes go into a heated holding oven at the temperature the maker gives. If they have been left out or have taken in moisture, they are re-dried in a drying oven exactly as the maker says, and only the number of times allowed, or scrapped. On the job, welders carry only a few electrodes at a time in a heated quiver, and keep the lid shut. Electrodes with damaged or cracked flux, or that have been dropped in water, are thrown away. The electrode type and batch number are checked against the WPS and written on the weld record. Different alloy grades must be kept apart and clearly labelled, so the wrong electrode is not used on the pipe.
markingPoints: Moisture brings hydrogen which causes cracking
Dry store, then a heated holding oven at the maker's temperature
Re-dry as the maker says, or scrap; damaged flux thrown away
Heated quiver, small quantities on the job
Check type and batch against the WPS; keep grades apart and labelled

essays.stem: Describe how you would prepare and fit up two alloy steel pipe ends for a 6G butt weld to a WPS.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would check the pipe markings and heat number against the mill certificate and the drawing, so the material is right, and transfer the markings onto each cut piece. I would cut the pipe square by machine or saw, then bevel each end to the angle in the WPS, often 37.5°, and grind a root face to the size given. I would clean the bevels and about 25 mm inside and outside back to bright metal, removing all rust, scale, oil and paint. I would check the bevel angle and root face with a gauge. I would set the pipes in a line-up clamp with spacers to give the root gap the WPS states, and check the alignment with a hi-lo gauge, keeping it within the limit. I would preheat to the WPS before tacking, then tack with the same electrode as the root, making small, sound tacks spaced around the pipe and grinding their ends to a taper. I would record the fit-up checks before welding.
markingPoints: Checks material identity and transfers markings
Cuts square, bevels to the WPS angle, grinds root face
Cleans bevels inside and out to bright metal; gauges the bevel
Sets root gap and checks hi-lo within the limit
Preheats before tacking; sound, tapered tacks; records fit-up

essays.stem: Describe how preheat and interpass temperatures are applied, measured and recorded on an alloy steel pipe joint.
essays.modelAnswer: Preheat is applied evenly all round the joint, over the band the WPS gives on each side, using electric heating pads, an induction coil or a gas heating torch. With a torch, the flame is kept moving so that no spot overheats. The temperature is measured on the parent metal, at the distance from the joint that the WPS gives, and on the side away from the heat source where possible, after the heat has had time to soak through. It can be measured with a temperature crayon, a contact thermometer or a calibrated infrared thermometer. It is checked in several places round the pipe. Before each new pass, the interpass temperature is checked to make sure it is above the minimum preheat and below the maximum. If it is too hot, the welder waits; if it has cooled, it is heated again. Readings are written on the weld and heat log with the time, the place measured, the method and the name of the person checking.
markingPoints: Even heating over the band given in the WPS; method named
Measured on parent metal at the given distance after soaking
Tools: crayon, contact thermometer, calibrated infrared
Interpass checked before each pass; wait or reheat as needed
Recorded with time, place, method and name

essays.stem: Describe how you would weld an alloy steel pipe butt joint in the 5G position with low-hydrogen electrodes, from the root to the cap.
essays.modelAnswer: With the pipe fixed and preheated to the WPS, I would start the root just past the bottom (6 o'clock) and weld uphill to just past the top (12 o'clock) on one side, then do the other side, overlapping the starts and stops. I would use a short arc and a steady, slight side-to-side movement, watching the keyhole so that both edges fuse and the root penetrates evenly. I would change the electrode angle as I move round the pipe. Before tying in, I would grind the starts and stops to a taper. I would clean the root fully, grind any high spots and run the hot pass to burn out trapped slag. For the fill passes I would use a limited weave or stringer beads, cleaning each pass and checking the interpass temperature. The cap would be a weave slightly past the bevel edges, even and with no undercut. Between passes I would strike the arc only in the groove.
markingPoints: Preheated; uphill from 6 to 12 o'clock on each side
Short arc, keyhole, changing electrode angle round the pipe
Starts and stops ground to a taper for tie-ins
Cleaning, hot pass, limited weave fills, interpass checks
Even cap just past the bevel edges; strikes only in the groove

essays.stem: Explain the purpose of heat treatment after welding (PWHT) on Cr-Mo pipe, what the WPS sets for it, and how it is controlled and recorded.
essays.modelAnswer: Heat treatment after welding tempers the hard, brittle zone next to the weld, making it tougher, and relieves the stresses locked in by welding. It also lets any remaining hydrogen escape. The WPS sets the heating rate, the holding temperature range, the holding time (often based on the wall thickness) and the cooling rate down to a set temperature. It also sets the width of the heated band and the insulation. The work is done by a trained, authorised operator with heating pads or a furnace. Thermocouples are fixed to the pipe at set places, and a recorder draws a chart of the temperature against time for the whole cycle. The chart is checked against the WPS limits and signed. If the cycle is interrupted or goes outside the limits, it is reported, and the engineer decides what must be done. The chart is kept with the joint's weld records, and a hardness test may be done afterwards to check the result.
markingPoints: Tempers the hard zone, relieves stress, lets hydrogen escape
WPS sets heating rate, holding temperature, time and cooling rate
Trained operator; thermocouples and a chart recorder
Chart checked, signed and kept; problems reported to the engineer
Hardness test may confirm the result

essays.stem: Describe how a welder's 6G pipe qualification test is usually carried out and assessed, and what the results mean.
essays.modelAnswer: The welder welds a pipe test coupon fixed at 45° to a qualified WPS, with an inspector watching the preparation, preheat and welding, and checking the settings and electrodes. When finished, the coupon is first inspected visually: the cap and root must be fully fused, the right size, and free of cracks, undercut beyond the limit, porosity and lack of penetration. If it passes, it is tested further, either by bend tests or by radiography, as the code allows. For bend tests, strips are cut from set places round the pipe so that each welding position is tested, and they are bent around a former. Any open flaws must be within the limits. If the coupon passes, the welder is qualified for a range of positions, diameters, thicknesses and electrode groups set by the code. A 6G test generally covers all positions. The results are written on a qualification record, which is signed and kept, and the welder must keep using the process to stay qualified.
markingPoints: Welds a 45° fixed coupon to a qualified WPS with an inspector watching
Visual inspection first
Bend tests from set positions, or radiography
Pass gives a range of positions and sizes; 6G generally covers all positions
Results recorded and signed; qualification kept current

essays.stem: Describe the hazards of preheating, welding and heat treating alloy steel pipe at the Centre, and the controls for each.
essays.modelAnswer: Preheating and heat treatment make the pipe very hot for a long time, so there is a high risk of burns. The pipe must be marked hot, barriers put up, and heat-resistant gloves worn. Gas heating torches bring fire and gas leak risks: hoses are checked, flashback arrestors fitted, the flame kept away from hoses and combustibles, and an extinguisher kept close. Electric heating pads carry a shock risk and must only be set up by a trained operator. Insulation blankets can give off fibres, so gloves and a dust mask are worn when handling them. Arc welding brings UV light, so screens, a helmet with the correct shade and covered skin are needed. The fume contains chromium and manganese, so local extraction is used and a respirator if needed. Electric shock is controlled by checking cables and keeping PPE dry. Pipe lengths are heavy, so team lifts or lifting aids are used. Heat stress is a real risk in Jamaica's climate, so water and rest breaks are planned.
markingPoints: Burns from hot pipe: mark hot, barriers, heat-resistant gloves
Gas torch and electric pad risks with controls
Insulation fibres; UV; fume with chromium and manganese
Electric shock and manual handling controls
Heat stress: water and rest breaks; Centre rules

essays.stem: Describe how you would visually inspect a finished alloy steel pipe weld and what you would put in the inspection report.
essays.modelAnswer: I would wait until the joint is cool enough, or wear suitable gloves, and make sure there is good light. I would check that the weld number and welder's mark are on the pipe. I would look at the cap all round the pipe for cracks, porosity, undercut, overlap, arc strikes and spatter, and check the cap width and height with a weld gauge against the code limits. Where I can see the root, with a mirror or a torch, I would check for full penetration, root concavity, excess penetration and burn-through. I would check the alignment of the pipe and that no hi-lo has opened up. I would check that the heat log shows preheat and interpass were within the WPS. In the report I would give the job and joint number, welder, WPS, electrode batch, date, each check made with the result, any defect with its size and position (using clock positions), and whether the weld is accepted, rejected or sent for further testing. I would sign and date it.
markingPoints: Good light, identifies the joint and welder
Checks the cap for surface faults and measures size with a gauge
Checks the root where visible and the alignment
Checks the heat log
Report: details, results, defects with clock position, decision, signed and dated

essays.stem: You lead a team of three welders on an alloy steel pipe spool job to an AWS specification. Explain how you would plan, run and check the work.
essays.modelAnswer: I would read the drawings, the specification and the WPS, and list the joints on a weld map. I would check that each welder is qualified for the positions and pipe sizes, and give each one joints that suit their qualification. I would check the materials and electrodes against the certificates and the WPS, and make sure the ovens, heating equipment and welding sets are working. I would plan the order of work so that each joint can be preheated, welded and kept warm without long breaks, and arrange heat treatment. At a toolbox talk I would brief the team on the WPS, hot work, fume control, heat stress and the hold points. During the job I would check fit-ups before welding, check preheat and interpass logs, and inspect roots before the next pass. I would deal with any problem at once and report anything outside the WPS. At the end I would make sure inspection and test records are complete, and write a report to my supervisor.
markingPoints: Reads drawings, specification and WPS; makes a weld map
Matches joints to welders' qualifications; checks materials and equipment
Plans the sequence and heat treatment; briefs the team on safety and hold points
Checks fit-up, preheat logs and roots during the job
Completes records and reports; deals with problems promptly

practical1.title: Preheat and weld a low-alloy steel pipe butt joint in the 5G or 6G position to a WPS
practical1.brief: As a team, read the WPS the assessor gives you for MMAW on low-alloy (Cr-Mo) steel pipe, or on the steel pipe the Centre stocks, and write a short work plan: the preparation, the preheat method and temperature, the interpass limit, the electrode type and size, the passes, the hold points and who does what. Check the pipe markings and the electrodes in the oven against the WPS. Prepare and bevel two pipe ends, clean them and fit them up in a line-up clamp with the root gap and alignment in the WPS. Preheat the joint, check the temperature, and tack it. Weld the joint in the position the assessor sets (5G or 6G), uphill, with members taking turns: each member runs at least one pass (root, hot pass, fill or cap) while the assessor watches. Another member checks and records the preheat or interpass temperature before every pass on a heat log. When finished, wrap the joint for slow cooling if the WPS says so. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the joint, the heat log and the clean-up are finished.
materials: Two lengths of low-alloy (or carbon) steel pipe, about 150 mm long, size and wall as the assessor gives
WPS from the assessor, plan sheet and heat log
MMAW set with DC output, low-hydrogen electrodes (E8018-B2 or as the WPS states) in a holding oven and quiver
Pipe bevelling equipment or oxy-fuel cutting set, angle grinder with grinding and cutting discs
Line-up clamp, spacers, bevel gauge, hi-lo gauge, weld gauge
Heating torch or electric heating pads, temperature crayons or contact thermometer
photos: The work plan and the WPS
The pipe markings and the electrodes in the oven being checked
The bevelled ends with gauges showing the angle and root face
The joint in the line-up clamp, preheated, with a temperature check
A member running the root in full PPE
The finished cap all round the pipe
checklist: Helped plan the job and read the WPS correctly
Checked the material and electrodes against the WPS
Prepared a bevel and root face within the WPS ranges
Set the root gap and alignment within the limits
Preheated evenly and checked the temperature correctly
Ran a sound pass with correct technique and cleaned it fully
Recorded preheat or interpass temperatures accurately
Wore full PPE throughout and left the area safe and tidy
safety: Mark hot pipe clearly and put up a barrier; wear heat-resistant gloves
Keep gas hoses away from the heating flame and the hot pipe; keep an extinguisher close
Use local fume extraction: alloy steel fume contains chromium and manganese
Wear a face shield and safety glasses when grinding
Drink water and take rest breaks: preheated work in Jamaica's heat can cause heat stress
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules

practical2.title: Inspect and test pipe weld coupons and write an inspection report
practical2.brief: As a team, inspect and test welded pipe coupons: the joint from Practical 1 or coupons the assessor gives you. First, plan the inspection: the checks, the gauges and tests, the acceptance limits the assessor gives you from the specification, and who does what. Carry out a full visual inspection: mark clock positions on the pipe, and check and measure the cap, the root where it can be seen, undercut, alignment and any faults. Check the heat log against the WPS. Mark out and cut bend test strips from the positions the assessor shows, prepare their edges, and bend them in the Centre's bend tester as the assessor directs (or, if there is no bend tester, make nick-break tests as the assessor directs). Inspect the tested strips and measure any openings. Each member carries out at least one inspection check and one test step. Write an inspection report with a sketch, your results and a decision for each coupon: accept, reject or repair. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the report is finished and the area is clean.
materials: Welded pipe coupons (from Practical 1 or from the assessor)
Acceptance limits from the assessor, inspection report sheets
Weld gauges, hi-lo gauge, steel rule, mirror and torch, magnifying glass
Bandsaw or cut-off saw, angle grinder and files to prepare strips
Bend tester or press as the Centre has (or vice and hammer for nick-break tests)
photos: The inspection plan and acceptance limits
The coupon marked with clock positions
A weld gauge measuring the cap
